aic:36660.summary: On one face of this gold coin Christ sits frontally on a throne, haloed, holding the book of the Gospels, with a Latin legend proclaiming him King of rulers. On the other face the Virgin crowns the Emperor Romanos III Argyros, who holds a cross-topped orb. Passed from hand to hand across the empire, such coins proclaimed that the emperor ruled under Christ, the true King.
facts: Romanos III Argyros reigned 1028–1034; the Art Institute notes that he died possibly at the hands, or on the order, of his wife Zoe.
The legend around Christ reads IhS XIS REX REGNANTIUM ('Jesus Christ, King of those who reign').
The coin is about 2.5 cm in diameter.

links.label: Art Institute of Chicago: object page

aic:36660.notes: Place given by the museum as 'Istanbul'; changed to the historical name Constantinople. The museum's text says Christ holds the Gospel book in his right hand, but in the photograph he holds it in his left, with the right hand at his breast.

cur:manuscripts-khludov-christ-above-dav.summary: On this damaged frontispiece, David the psalmist sits beneath a broad arch on a column, while above him, set within the arch, a large medallion contains the bust of Christ. Small figures stand at either side. Placing Christ above David at the opening of the Psalter presents the psalms as words that look forward to him.
facts: The Russian Orthodox Encyclopedia, the source of the image, identifies it as folio 1v of the manuscript.
The Psalter was kept on Mount Athos until 1847, when it was taken to Moscow; it later belonged to the merchant Aleksey Khludov, whose name it bears.

cur:manuscripts-soissons-gospels-adorati.summary: At the top of a monumental architectural frontispiece, the Lamb of God stands in a medallion against the heavens while the twenty-four elders, in two groups, rise from their seats and raise their crowns toward him. Below, the four evangelist symbols appear in roundels on a cornice, and beneath that a great curtained façade on columns opens like the entrance to a heavenly sanctuary. Christ is shown here in the symbolic form of the Apocalypse, the Lamb who was slain.
facts: The manuscript was given to the abbey of Saint-Médard at Soissons by Louis the Pious and his wife Judith in 827 and remained there until the French Revolution.
It belongs to the Court or 'Ada' School of Charlemagne; besides twelve decorated canon tables it has six full-page miniatures, including a Fountain of Life modelled on the Godescalc Evangelistary.

links.label: Wikipedia: Gospels of Saint Médard of Soissons

cur:manuscripts-soissons-gospels-adorati.notes: Christ is shown symbolically as the Lamb of the Apocalypse.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-73-christ.summary: In the upper right corner the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos sits on a globe atop a high mountain, Sion, with 'the sheep of thy pasture' on a ledge below him. The young psalmist raises his hands for deliverance while lions and bears climb toward him, and the sun, moon, summer and winter fill the sky. The psalm laments the ruin of the sanctuary, but Christ remains enthroned above it.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-73-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects-magdeburg-ivory-trial-flagel.summary: Two moments of the Passion share this openwork plaque: at the left Christ is bound to a column and scourged by soldiers, while at the right Pilate, seated beneath a curtain, washes his hands as a servant pours water. Christ, taller than his tormentors and haloed, remains calm and upright. The pierced plant and architectural background is typical of the Magdeburg series.
facts: The Magdeburg Ivories show an unusual emphasis on Christ's ministry, and two further panels are known only from 16th-century drawings (Wikipedia).
The photographer's caption identifies this plaque as one of the reliefs donated to Magdeburg Cathedral by Otto I, made in Milan between 962 and 973.

walters:71.194.summary: On the left leaf, the Virgin reclines in bed, her head resting on her hand, beside the swaddled Christ Child in his woven crib, while Joseph sits nearby and shepherds and their flock receive the angel's news on the hillside above. On the right leaf, the crowned Virgin presents the standing Child to the three kings, the eldest kneeling with his gift and another pointing to the star. Each scene is set under three trefoil arches.
facts: The Walters notes that the two scenes are based on the large Passion diptychs, such as Walters 71.272, and relates details to works attributed to Mosan or Flemish artists.
Each leaf is only about 7.3 by 5.4 cm; both are cracked vertically and one has been rejoined.
